steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning has evolved and brought major changes to a lot of fields in the past few decades. In recent years large language models (LLMs) have appeared and revolutionized the field of natural language processing, and they have also brought big changes to many other areas. Since access to ChatGPT became publicly available in late 2022, the number of users has been rocketing, and so has the number of publicly-available services that use LLM APIs provided by OpenAI. These models have shown they can understand and process inputs including but not limited to natural languages, and they have been used for different types of tasks. A typical use of LLMs is text generation, since they can produce high-quality natural language outputs. This caused a heated debate in academia and in the end major publishers announced new regulations about using generative AI. LLMs have also shown extraordinary potential in programming tasks, including code generation and code comprehension. LLM-based assistant tools like Github Copilot have got tremendous attention and are widely used by programmers all around the world. Recently OpenAI enabled more features in ChatGPT, which makes LLMs more versatile and able to do more real-world tasks.

Among all the possibilities of LLMs, code analysis and obfuscation are getting more and more attention from computer scientists. Code analysis is an important task in software engineering, and includes code quality assessment, vulnerabilities detection, etc. Modern software systems are huge and have complex architectures, so automated code analysis is widely used, especially in security-related scenarios like software reverse engineering. In response, malicious parties have used code obfuscation techniques to obscure source code and avoid being detected. Researchers in turn have proposed automated code analysis tools like Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to analyze both non-obfuscated and obfuscated code. But these tools depend heavily on pre-defined data types and are not suitable for general software code analysis. Because LLMs have great potential in these areas, researchers have started to use LLMs for related tasks. However, a recent survey points out that there are few systematic analytical studies on this topic.

- Our study
  - evaluate LLMs analyzing input code; usable for defensive analysis tasks?
  - dataset of real-world programs (Github, etc.) + obfuscated versions; analyze outcomes, key findings
  - RQs: Do LLMs understand source code? Can LLMs comprehend obfuscated code or code with low readability?
  - case studies: publicly-available LLMs (e.g. ChatGPT) on real-world malicious software
- Contributions
  - 1. two datasets (popular languages + obfuscated samples)
  - 2. systematic evaluation, GPT and LLaMA families
  - 3. case studies on real-world malicious software
  - first systematic evaluation of this kind
- Organization: Sections 2-8; online appendix https://github.com/aseec-lab/llms-for-code-analysis

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning has evolved and brought major changes to a lot of fields in the past few decades. In recent years large language models (LLMs) have appeared and revolutionized the field of natural language processing, and they have also brought big changes to many other areas. Since access to ChatGPT became publicly available in late 2022, the number of users has been rocketing, and so has the number of publicly-available services that use LLM APIs provided by OpenAI. These models have shown they can understand and process inputs including but not limited to natural languages, and they have been used for different types of tasks. A typical use of LLMs is text generation, since they can produce high-quality natural language outputs. This caused a heated debate in academia and in the end major publishers announced new regulations about using generative AI. LLMs have also shown extraordinary potential in programming tasks, including code generation and code comprehension. LLM-based assistant tools like Github Copilot have got tremendous attention and are widely used by programmers all around the world. Recently OpenAI enabled more features in ChatGPT, which makes LLMs more versatile and able to do more real-world tasks.

Among all the possibilities of LLMs, code analysis and obfuscation are getting more and more attention from computer scientists. Code analysis is an important task in software engineering, and includes code quality assessment, vulnerabilities detection, etc. Modern software systems are huge and have complex architectures, so automated code analysis is widely used, especially in security-related scenarios like software reverse engineering. In response, malicious parties have used code obfuscation techniques to obscure source code and avoid being detected. Researchers in turn have proposed automated code analysis tools like Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to analyze both non-obfuscated and obfuscated code. But these tools depend heavily on pre-defined data types and are not suitable for general software code analysis. Because LLMs have great potential in these areas, researchers have started to use LLMs for related tasks. However, a recent survey points out that there are few systematic analytical studies on this topic.

In this paper we evaluate the ability of LLMs to analyze input code samples, and test whether LLMs can be used for defensive analysis tasks. First we build a dataset with code from real-world programs (on Github, etc.) and obfuscated versions of it to feed to LLMs, and then we analyze the outcomes and present the key findings we got. Through a systematic analysis we want to answer two critical research questions:

Do LLMs understand source code?

Can LLMs comprehend obfuscated code or code with low readability?

Then, as real-world case studies, we show whether publicly-available LLMs (e.g. ChatGPT) can be used for security-related tasks on real-world malicious software.

Our contributions are:

- 1. We build two datasets with code samples from popular programming languages and obfuscated samples from these languages for our evaluation;

- 2. We systematically evaluate publicly available state-of-the-art LLMs, including the GPT and LLaMA families which are the most popularly used, on our dataset, and present our findings;

- 3. We do case studies using LLMs to analyze real-world malicious software, to show what LLMs can and cannot do in these tasks.

As far as we know, this is the first paper that systematically evaluates the ability of LLMs to comprehend code and code with obfuscation.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 introduces related background knowledge. Section 3 explains our experiment settings for the analysis. Section 4 presents the essential results and findings. In Section 5 we do case studies and show how LLMs can help code analysis in practical cases. Section 6 briefly discusses future works. Section 7 has related works and Section 8 the conclusion. Our online appendix is available at: https://github.com/aseec-lab/llms-for-code-analysis.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The evolution of machine learning has brought major changes to a variety of fields in the past few decades [1,2,3,4]. In recent years, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized the field of natural language processing and brought great changes to many other areas. Ever since access to ChatGPT [5] became publicly available in late 2022, there has been a rocketing number of users as well as publicly-available services utilizing LLM APIs provided by OpenAI. These models have demonstrated their ability to understand and process inputs including but not limited to natural languages, and have been involved in different types of tasks. A typical use case of LLMs is text generation, since they can produce high-quality natural language outputs [6]. This has caused a heated debate in academia and eventually resulted in major publishers announcing new regulations regarding the usage of generative AI [7,8]. Besides, LLMs have also manifested extraordinary potential in programming-related tasks, including code generation [9] and code comprehension [10]. LLM-based assistant tools like Github Copilot [11] have received tremendous attention and are widely employed by programmers all around the world. OpenAI has recently enabled more features in ChatGPT [12], making LLMs more versatile and capable of engaging in more real-world tasks.

Amidst all possibilities of LLMs, code analysis and obfuscation are tasks receiving more and more attention from computer scientists. Code analysis [13] is an important task in software engineering, including code quality assessment [14], vulnerabilities detection [15], etc. The huge size and complex architecture of modern software systems motivate the wide usage of automated code analysis, especially in security-related scenarios such as software reverse engineering [16]. In response, malicious parties have leveraged code obfuscation techniques to obscure source code and avoid being detected, and researchers have proposed automated code analysis tools like Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) [17] to analyze both non-obfuscated and obfuscated code. However, such tools are highly dependent on pre-defined data types and are not suitable for general software code analysis. Given the great potential of LLMs in these areas, researchers have started using LLMs to perform related tasks [18,10]. However, as pointed out by a recent survey [19], there are few systematic analytical studies on this topic.

In this paper, we focus on evaluating the ability of LLMs to analyze input code samples, and test whether LLMs can be utilized for defensive analysis tasks. We first construct a dataset containing code from real-world programs (on Github, etc.) and their obfuscated versions to feed to LLMs, then analyze the outcomes and present our key findings. We aim to answer two critical research questions through a systematic analysis:

Do LLMs understand source code?

Can LLMs comprehend obfuscated code or code with low readability?

After that, as real-world case studies, we showcase whether publicly-available LLMs (e.g. ChatGPT) can be utilized for security-related tasks targeting real-world malicious software.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

- 1. We construct two datasets consisting of code samples from popular programming languages and obfuscated samples from these languages for our evaluation;

- 2. We systematically evaluate the performance of publicly available state-of-the-art LLMs, including the most popularly used GPT and LLaMA families, on our dataset, and present our findings;

- 3. We conduct case studies using LLMs to analyze real-world malicious software to showcase the capability and limitations of LLMs in these tasks.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to provide a systematic evaluation of the ability of LLMs to comprehend code and code with obfuscation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We introduce related background knowledge in Section 2, and elaborate the experiment settings of our analysis in Section 3. Essential results and findings are presented in Section 4. In Section 5, we perform case studies and show how LLMs can be utilized to assist code analysis in practical cases. We briefly discuss future works in Section 6. Related works and a conclusion are provided in Section 7 and Section 8, respectively. Our online appendix is available at: https://github.com/aseec-lab/llms-for-code-analysis.
